Should contractors use Facebook ads?

7 min read

Facebook ads can work for contractors, but they are not the right first move for everyone. They shine for visual, planned, and seasonal work where you can create demand — remodels, roofing after a storm, fencing, landscaping — and they fall flat for emergencies people search for the moment they happen. They only pay off if you follow up on leads fast, which is exactly where most contractors fail.

“Facebook ads are the best ROI in contracting — when done right.” You’ve heard some version of that, probably from someone trying to sell you Facebook ads. It’s not wrong, exactly. But that little phrase — when done right — is doing an enormous amount of work, and it’s where most contractors’ money quietly disappears.

So let’s answer the real question honestly: Facebook ads can absolutely work for contractors. They’re just the right tool for a specific job, and the wrong tool for others. Knowing which is which saves you thousands.

The fundamental difference: search vs. interruption

Here’s the concept that decides everything. Google captures demand. Facebook creates it.

When someone’s water heater bursts, they grab their phone and search “emergency plumber near me.” That’s demand that already exists — you just have to be there to catch it, which is a search game. Nobody scrolling Facebook with a coffee is thinking about their water heater. Facebook ads interrupt people who weren’t looking and plant an idea: “Huh, our deck does look rough. Maybe this spring.”

That single distinction tells you whether Facebook is right for your trade.

When Facebook ads work well for contractors

Facebook earns its keep when the work is visual, planned, and discretionary — the kind of project someone can be talked into rather than forced into:

  • Remodels and renovations — a stunning before-and-after photo stops the scroll cold.
  • Roofing after a storm — geo-target the neighborhoods that just got hit while it’s top of mind.
  • Fencing, decks, landscaping, hardscaping — visual, seasonal, and easy to inspire.
  • Bath and kitchen remodels — high-ticket and aspirational, which Facebook’s imagery sells well.

For these, a strong photo plus a clear offer, tightly geo-targeted to your service area, can fill a pipeline — especially for smoothing out the feast-or-famine cycle. Roofers in particular know the pattern: leads pour in after a storm, then go dead for weeks. Facebook can help fill those quiet stretches by creating demand instead of waiting for it.

When Facebook ads disappoint

Facebook struggles where the work is an urgent, unplanned emergency. If your bread and butter is burst pipes, no heat in January, or electrical failures, your customer isn’t scrolling — they’re searching, right now, ready to hire. For those trades your money is far better spent owning search: a strong Google Business Profile, local rankings, and high-intent Google Ads that appear at the exact moment of need.

It also disappoints anyone hoping for instant booked jobs. Facebook leads are colder than search leads — the person was interested enough to fill out a form, but they weren’t actively shopping. They need nurturing, and that brings us to the part that makes or breaks the whole thing.

The make-or-break factor: follow-up speed

This is where most Facebook ad budgets die, and it has nothing to do with the ads. A Facebook lead is interested for about five minutes. If you call back the next morning, that interest is gone — they’ve moved on, forgotten they even filled out the form, or hired whoever called first.

Remember that 66% of home-services businesses name lead follow-up and conversion as a top challenge, and that the average home-services business misses 30 to 40% of its calls during busy periods. Now pair that with paid leads you bought, and the leak becomes expensive. Pour money into ads, then let half the leads go cold, and you’ve funded a very efficient way to lose money.

If you can’t guarantee a near-instant response — including evenings and weekends, when a lot of homeowners actually browse — fix that before you spend a dollar on ads. An AI receptionist or instant-response system can catch those leads the moment they come in, and we cover the broader cost of dropping them in how missed calls are costing your business money.

The honest verdict

Should you run Facebook ads? Maybe — if your work is visual and discretionary, if you can target tightly, and if you’ll follow up fast. But for most contractors, the smarter sequence is: own your search visibility first, build a system to respond to leads instantly, then layer Facebook on top to create demand and fill the slow weeks. Ads built on a leaky foundation just leak faster. See where everything fits in the best lead sources for contractors.

One more reality check before you commit a budget: Facebook ads are not a set-and-forget channel. Creative fatigues, audiences burn out, and the offer that crushed it in spring goes quiet by midsummer. The contractors who win on Facebook are the ones who refresh photos, test new offers, and watch their cost per booked job — not just their cost per lead — every few weeks. If that ongoing attention sounds like more than you want to manage, that is itself a strong signal to put your money where it compounds on its own: search visibility and reviews that keep working long after you stop paying.

Frequently asked questions

Do Facebook ads actually work for contractors?

They can, for the right trade and with fast follow-up. Facebook ads work best for visual, planned, discretionary work like remodels, roofing, fencing, and landscaping, where a strong photo and clear offer can create demand. They disappoint for urgent emergency work, which people search for instead, and they waste money if leads are not contacted almost immediately.

Are Facebook ads better than Google Ads for contractors?

It depends on your work. Google captures demand that already exists, so it wins for emergency and high-intent searches like burst pipes or no heat. Facebook creates demand by interrupting people who were not looking, so it wins for visual, planned projects. Many contractors do best owning search first, then layering Facebook on top to fill slow stretches.

Why do contractors lose money on Facebook ads?

Usually because of slow follow-up. A Facebook lead is interested for only a few minutes, and if you call back the next morning the interest is gone. With 66% of home-services businesses naming lead conversion a top challenge and 30 to 40% of calls missed during busy periods, paid leads that go cold turn ad spend into wasted money.

How fast do I need to respond to Facebook leads?

Nearly instantly, ideally within minutes, including evenings and weekends when many homeowners browse. Facebook leads are colder than search leads because the person was not actively shopping, so any delay lets that interest fade. An AI receptionist or instant-response system can catch leads the moment they arrive so none go to waste.
